book.title: Essentialism: The Disciplined Pursuit of Less
book.author: Greg McKeown

confidence_note: Kept: McKeown's argument that every choice is a trade-off, his use of Derek Sivers's 'hell yeah or no' idea, and his rule that if the answer isn't a clear yes it is a clear no (his 90 percent rule for applying selective criteria). The speaking-invitation example in the reference text is an illustration, not from the book, and is omitted; the quoted line 'saying yes to good opportunities means missing excellent ones' is paraphrase, not a verified quote. Paraphrased from recall; not checked against the text.
facts: McKeown argues that trade-offs are unavoidable: choosing one thing always means not choosing something else, whether we admit it or not.
He asks the reader to stop asking 'How can I do both?' and instead ask 'Which problem do I want?' when options compete.
He cites entrepreneur Derek Sivers's rule: if you are not saying 'Hell yeah!' about something, say no.

McKeown turns this into a selection rule: if the answer isn't a clear yes, it's a clear no. He also describes it as a 90 percent rule: score an option against your most important criterion, and if it falls below about 90, treat it as a zero.
The point is that mostly-fine opportunities, accepted automatically, take the time and energy that the rare excellent ones need.
tension: A good opportunity is hardest to refuse precisely because nothing is wrong with it.
opening_idea: An offer arrives that is decent on every count. McKeown's test does not ask whether it is good, only whether your first reaction is an unmistakable 'Hell yeah!'

lessons.idea: Every yes is also a no to something you may not yet see.
lessons.anchor: McKeown's point that trade-offs cannot be avoided

lessons.idea: Raising the bar for yes protects room for the best options.
lessons.anchor: The 'clear yes or clear no' / 90 percent rule

lessons.idea: Hesitation is information about how much you really want something.

reflect: Which recent yes did you give because the offer was fine rather than because you wanted it?
What did that yes quietly take time away from?
reflect_final: The next time you receive an invitation or request, give it an honest score against your main priority before answering, and notice how many fall short of a clear yes.

use_cases.situation: A stakeholder asks your team to take on a reasonable extra project.
use_cases.move: Ask the room what current work would be dropped to make space, so the trade-off is named before anyone agrees.

use_cases.situation: A friend invites you to join a group commitment that sounds pleasant but not exciting.
use_cases.move: Use Sivers's test on yourself: since your reaction isn't a 'hell yeah', thank them warmly and decline this one.

use_cases.situation: You're weighing an offer that looks good on paper.
use_cases.move: Score it from 0 to 100 against the one criterion that matters most to you; if it lands below about 90, treat it as a no and see how that feels.

pocket_idea: If it isn't 'Hell yeah!', it's no: a lukewarm yes spends the space an excellent option would need.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: McKeown's rule for opportunities: anything that scores 89 out of 100 counts as zero.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: McKeown borrows Derek Sivers's rule, 'if it's not hell yeah, it's no', and sharpens it: rate an option against your top criterion and if it isn't a clear yes, it's a clear no, because every yes is a trade-off against something better.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What's something you said yes to because it was 'fine', and what would you have done with that time instead?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: Saying yes because nothing is wrong versus saying yes only when you really want it.
